ID: villa-tugendhat

WIDER CONTEXT
- In January 2007 descendants of the Tugendhat family officially petitioned the Brno city authorities and the Culture Ministry for the return of the villa, which the Gestapo had taken over and the Czechoslovak state confiscated in 1945 (Radio Prague International, 9 January 2007).
- In February 2007 Brno City Hall criticised the family for selling Wilhelm Lehmbruck's "Torso of a Walking Woman", which had stood in the villa and had been returned to them the year before, at Sotheby's in London to an anonymous foreign bidder for one million pounds. City spokesman Pavel Zara said "the sale of the statue signals that the fate of the villa may not meet our expectations". The family said a statue could not be compared to the building and that part of the proceeds would have paid for repairs had the villa been returned to them (Radio Prague International, 7 February 2007).
- In March 2007, less than two months after deciding to transfer the villa to the state so it could be returned to the heirs, the Brno City Council and assembly voted to keep it as city property after the state rejected the procedure. The city said the law under which it was claimed covers works of art, not immovable property, and that a donation would have triggered gift tax of hundreds of millions of crowns. The family's lawyer Augustin Kohoutek said the assembly "changed its opinion 180 degrees" and that "the family will very likely start a court action for the return of the villa" (Radio Prague International, 21 March 2007).

WIDER CONTEXT
- The historian Martin Jindra of the Institute for the Study of Totalitarian Regimes writes that after the communist takeover the Bílek family was pressed by political conditions into transferring the villa to the state. Berta Mildová-Bílková negotiated the transfer from the 1950s, and it was completed in 1963 together with the artworks, with the Prague City Gallery as the new owner (Seznam Zprávy, Martin Jindra, 7 March 2026).
- Jindra writes that the new owner then charged the two women living there rent for the kitchen and three first-floor rooms: "Nemorálně a nelidsky jednající režim okamžitě po nabytí majetku vyměřil „nájemnicím" finanční částku za obývání kuchyně a tří místností v prvním patře" ("The immorally and inhumanly acting regime, immediately after acquiring the property, charged the 'tenants' a sum for living in the kitchen and three rooms on the first floor", translated). Central heating was refused for their rooms on the stated ground that "kapacita kotelny je tak nízká, že vytápění bytu Berty Bílkové ústředním topením nepřichází v úvahu" ("the boiler room's capacity is so low that heating Berta Bílková's flat by central heating is out of the question", translated) (Seznam Zprávy, 7 March 2026).
